title: Who was Moses?
summary: Exodus portrays Moses as the person God calls to confront Pharaoh and lead Israel out of Egypt. At Sinai he stands between the people and the covenant instruction, and Deuteronomy ends by remembering him as an exceptional prophet. Later texts recall him in ways that do not all make the same point.
historical_context: The cited biblical passages tell Moses’ story from his call and Israel’s deliverance through the Sinai encounter to his death in Deuteronomy. Matthew 17 and Hebrews 3 later present him in distinct settings. These references describe the scriptural account; this entry has no separate historical source for dating Moses or reconstructing the exodus.
canonical_context: Exodus 3 recounts Moses’ call; Exodus 12 narrates the Passover and Israel’s departure; Exodus 19–20 brings the people to Sinai and presents covenant instruction. Deuteronomy 34 closes Moses’ life by calling him an unmatched prophet in Israel. In Matthew 17, Moses appears with Elijah at Jesus’ transfiguration and the voice directs the disciples to listen to Jesus. Hebrews 3 compares Moses’ faithfulness as a servant in God’s house with Jesus’ role as Son over it. The later texts remember Moses in different ways.
literary_context: The Exodus narrative moves from Moses’ call to deliverance and then to the Sinai encounter; the cited chapters show how these events shape his role in the story. Deuteronomy 34 serves as a closing account of Moses’ death and legacy. Matthew 17 is a transfiguration scene, while Hebrews 3 is an argument comparing Moses and Jesus. Reading those passages by genre keeps the later references from becoming one undifferentiated claim about Moses.
covenantal_significance: Moses is central to the Exodus account of deliverance and the giving of covenant instruction at Sinai, but the text presents God as the one who calls, rescues, and establishes the covenant. Hebrews 3 honors Moses’ faithfulness while distinguishing his role as servant from Jesus’ role as Son. Matthew 17 directs the disciples to listen to Jesus. These later passages make specific claims about Moses and Jesus rather than saying simply that Moses’ whole life is fulfilled in Christ.
canonical_role: Who was Moses? serves as a question-oriented anchor, connecting common reader language to related passages, themes, and CKL entries.

interpretive_notes.note: Exodus 12 connects Moses’ leadership with Israel’s deliverance, and Exodus 19–20 places him at the Sinai covenant encounter. Deuteronomy 34 remembers him as an unmatched prophet. These passages show how the biblical narrative joins rescue, instruction, and prophetic leadership without making Moses the source of Israel’s covenant.

The later passages use Moses differently: Matthew 17 places him in the transfiguration scene, and Hebrews 3 compares his faithfulness as a servant with Jesus’ role as Son. Those texts support these particular connections; they do not establish a general pattern of Moses’ life as a template for every later deliverance.
